sections.text: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद् दृढम्।
My Lord! Verily, the mind is fickle and turbulent, obstinate and strong, yea extremely difficult as the wind to control.
Lord Shri Krishna replied: Doubtless, O Mighty One, the mind is fickle and exceedingly difficult to restrain, but, O Son of Kunti, with practice and renunciation it can be done.
असंयतात्मना योगो दुष्प्राप इति मे मतिः।
It is not possible to attain Self-Realisation if a man does not know how to control himself; but for him who, striving by proper means, learns such control, it is possible.

We have been discussing Chapter 6, Dhyana Yoga, Yoga of Meditation and Contemplation. So far we have seen in chapter 6 that Bhagavan has emphasized the quiet mind. The basis of all the practices is the mind.
As long as you can control the mind, you can become a yogi. Bhagavan had said Samatvam Yoga Uchyate -- equanimity is yoga. In this chapter he also says Duhkha Samyoga Viyoga is Yoga.
The detachment from the attachment to pain is Yoga. We have a natural attachment to pain; our mind goes towards pain more than it goes towards other things. Another way to look at it: detachment from all objects which have the potential to give me pain.
This is what we try to do in life -- avoid all the dangers, protect ourselves from any potential danger. But if you can detach yourself from all potential dangers, which actually includes all sense objects in this world -- all sense objects have equal capacity to give me pleasure as they have the capacity to give me pain. So therefore, if I really want to detach myself from all pains, all potential dangers of getting pain, I have to avoid all sense objects.
So in verse 27, Bhagawan has concluded his teachings. Prasantamanasamhi enam yoginam Sukha Muthamam. That supreme bliss which I am seeking all my life.
I am looking for permanent happiness. I dont want temporary happiness, I want permanent happiness. Bhagawan saying that happiness is available to a yogi who has achieved this supremely quiet mind.
Upeti Santarajasam Brahmabhutam or Kalmasam. Supreme bliss comes to this yogi whose mind is peaceful, whose patience are quietened and he does not have any rajas in Brahma Bhutam or Kalmasam. He has become sinless.
There is no impurity on his mind. It has become Brahman Brahma Bhutam. He recognizes that his own self, the ego, is none other than Brahman.
This synchronization of the ego with Brahman is the ultimate goal -- to achieve that final state of supreme happiness, permanent bliss. But the basis of all that is prasantamana. It all boils down to whether I can have this mind completely quiet, completely under control.
In verses 28 through 32, Bhagavan has described the yogi who has achieved this state of becoming Brahman. He sees that self in all beings and all beings in the self. He will have both perspective at the same time that he sees that consciousness in me.
But Im also in the consciousness. Pot space is within the spot, but pot is in the space also. That dual perspective, if I can have simultaneously, I can synchronize these two perspectives.
Bhagavan said that comes only when the Yogi has achieved this Siddhi of quietening the mind and becoming Brahman. He sees sameness everywhere. He never gets separated from the self, the self never gets separated from him.
Once the pot space realizes that the space outside me is no different, then the space within me never gets separated from the main space. When my ego recognizes that myself, the consciousness in me, is none other than the consciousness everywhere. So right now we cannot imagine that consciousness can be anything outside living beings.
But Bhagavad Gita time and again tells us that consciousness is all pervading. We are all existing within the consciousness. This world is created out of that supreme self.
There is no other material was available to create this universe other than the self alone. And because that yogi has achieved this state, he sees sameness of the self in all beings. Now he has achieved a different reason.
Our vision right now is to live in this world by identifying the differences. So the way we transact in this world is if I can detect differences, then I can differentiate things one from another. Table is not chair, chair is not table.
Because they will both look completely different from each other. Different characteristics. But I can also see probably the sameness if both are made up of wood.
That sameness when a person sees, it in the biblical term of that that person. Now because this is the sameness, he loves others as he loves his own self. I dont see any difference between doing something for me or doing something for others.
Its basically one and the same thing. Now I also wont do anything to others which I dont want others to do to me because of the sameness that I detect in all things and beings. Up till now I was seeing only differences and thats how I lived my life.
By detecting differences and protecting myself from what I dont find conducive and then engaging myself in what I find conducive. But now I dont say anything conducive or unconducive. But sameness is my central vision.
And Arjuna has been very quietly listening to this and he has come to the conclusion that the basis of all this is Prasantamanah supremely peaceful mind. And therefore he actually verbalize doubt we have in our mind while learning Bhagavad Gita whether it is at all possible. Arjunava Yoyam Yoga TV this yoga that you just described which can be achieved only by quiet mind.
Samyana Madhusudana of the sameness that you have described. The the yoga which you described which requires that I see sameness in everything and every being. We discussed the importance of the words used in our scriptures.
All the names used for Krishna or Arjuna are strategically placed. Madhusudana -- the slayer of the demon Madhu. In this life, we get attracted to things which are sweet for us, things which are nice and comfortable.
But attraction in the end creates all my sorrows. If I dont get attracted to them in the first place, I wont have the problems they are capable of giving me. Krishna as Madhusudana is the remover, the destroyer of this attraction to comfortable, pleasant things.
But Arjuna says, I dont see that happening. My mind always goes to finer things in life. I find Marriott is better, so I stay at Marriott, not at Super 8.
This is the nature of my mind. My mind always gravitates towards finer things and avoids painful, uncomfortable situations. I dont think thats going to change, because the very nature of the mind is ever-changing. The mind constantly flows in various directions, following whatever the sense organs report to it.
For example, when I was only experiencing Seven-Elevens coffee, my mind was satisfied with Seven-Elevens coffee. I remember when we used to practice bhajans in our youth group, wed invite a violin player named Subhas. As soon as he arrived, we had to send somebody to get his coffee from Seven-Eleven.
We couldnt offer him coffee at home -- Oh yeah, Subhas is here, go get his coffee from Seven-Eleven. Because for him 7 limits coffee was ultimate. The mind is chanchala -- as long as it has not experienced something better, it may stick to this. But as soon as it finds something better, its going to move on to the next thing and then the next thing.
Chanchalatva sthitim sthiram -- therefore I do not see this as a long-lasting situation, even if I practice everything that you taught me in this chapter about meditation. Find a quiet place, sit down comfortably and focus on one point. Then once I focus on one point, if your mind runs away, bring it back.
I may do it for 10 minutes, 20 minutes, 30 minutes. But what is after that? After that my mind is going to do exactly what it was doing before I sat down from meditation. So therefore, O Krishna, this is wonderful discourse.
But I dont think this is possible to achieve that permanent steadiness Prasantha Manasam which you have described in verse 27. This is a very bold and daring question because hes directly telling Krishna that this teaching is not practical. It sounds very good, it has good aesthetics, its pleasant to hear. But I dont see how to apply it in my life.
I know how my mind works, and its not going to stay in one place as you require. I think every one of us without exception feels exactly the same. We practice meditation -- how many minutes? We count meditation in minutes! But Bhagavan said it has to be a permanent situation. Your mind should be steady all the time.
Chanchalam hi manah Krishna, pramathi, balavad dridham -- he said, Im not giving you this argument just to make an argument. But I know the nature of the mind, my mind at least. Chanchalam hi manah Krishna -- this mind is always going in different directions. Pramathi -- its very turbulent.
Balavad dridham -- very strong and firm. Once my mind gets attached to an object, its very difficult to remove it. If I start thinking about drinking coffee, I wont be able to concentrate on what Im doing till I get a cup of coffee. Because the mind is very strong.
I have to get up and get a cup of coffee. You know, I can focus on whatever I was doing before. Then I put the coffee in that warmer I keep on my desk.
Then Ill forget about it. After an hour I realized that I got up, went and got a cup of coffee. The coffee was not really needed because I didnt even remember to drink it.
But at that time the mind was so attached to the coffee that I had to go get a cup. The word Krishna comes from the root Krish, which means to uproot. Krishna is the one who uproots all these attachments from my mind.
So Bhagavan Ved Vyasa very strategically placed this name. Arjuna has not addressed Krishna as Krishna casually. Chanchalam hi manah Krishna -- this mind is not only all over the place and going everywhere, but its very turbulent, very difficult to control.
And dridham -- when it gets attached to something, its very difficult to disengage it. Vayoh iva su-dushkaram -- not just dushkaram (difficult), but su-dushkaram (very difficult). I consider control of this mind as difficult as controlling the wind.
Right now we have a prediction of a hurricane hitting the upper east coast. All you can do is get out of its way. There is nothing you can say will prevent the hurricane from hitting New York or Long island.
Divert it towards the sea. None of that is in our power even though we are super power. Only thing you can do is get out of its way.
So this mind is as difficult to control as wind. And therefore, O Krishna, I dont think it is possible. Even if I control my mind temporarily, permanently it is not possible.
Therefore this yoga is not practical. Bhagavan then answers this question. We can learn a technique of how to win an argument. If we are debating or negotiating and somebody makes a point, and you flatly reject it, that person will become even firmer in his opinion.
Hell say, I dont agree with you, and that will continue. Nobody will win. So Bhagavan first agrees with Arjuna.
He said, You are right. The first thing you do is agree with your opponent. No doubt, you are not wrong, Arjuna. You are not making argument just for the sake of making an argument. But your argument is very, very valid. That mind is difficult to control.
This is a very commonly known fact. Mind is not easy to control.

Arjunas description of the mind in verse 34 is vivid and relatable: Chanchalam hi manah Krishna pramathi balavad dridham - the mind is restless, turbulent, strong, and obstinate. Once attached to an object, it clings stubbornly. You must get up for coffee, even if you forget to drink it afterward. Controlling such a mind seems vayoriva su-dushkaram - as difficult as controlling the wind. When hurricanes approach, all our technology is helpless; we can only step aside. Is the mind equally untameable?
Krishnas response in verse 35 is masterful. First, he agrees completely - Asamshayam mahabaho mano durnigraham chalam - without doubt, the mind is difficult to control. This is wise counsel for any disagreement: acknowledge the valid point before offering a different perspective. Then comes the prescription: Abhyasena tu Kaunteya vairagyena cha grihyate - through practice (abhyasa) and dispassion (vairagya), it can be mastered. Like circus animals trained to perform remarkable feats, like wild waters tamed by a dam to generate power, the very energy that makes the mind turbulent can be harnessed for spiritual awakening.
Verse 36 offers realistic assessment: Asamyatatmana yogo dushprapa - yoga is difficult for one with an uncontrolled self. But vashyatmana tu yatata shakyovaptum - for one who strives with a controlled self, using proper methods, it is attainable. The key is not extraordinary ability but consistent effort with the right approach. Today, choose one area where your mind is habitually uncontrolled - perhaps checking your phone, perhaps negative self-talk - and apply both abhyasa (repeatedly redirecting attention) and vairagya (reducing the pull of that habit). Small victories build the confidence that larger mastery is possible.
